articles.title: Anthropic tells investors quarterly revenue up nearly 50% to $16.8bn ahead of IPO
articles.summary: Anthropic tells investors quarterly revenue up nearly 50% to $16.8bn ahead of IPO The phrase "told investors" appears four times in this FT article, which reports on Anthropic's day of hosting investors on Wednesday. Lots of details in here from " people with knowledge of the matter ". Key things I learned from the article: Q1 revenue (Jan/Feb/Mar) was "about $4.8bn" Q2 (Apr/May/Jun) was $11.5bn Q3 (Jul/Aug/Sep) was $16.8bn In Q3: $1.70 in revenue for every $1 spent on "computing power" Adjusted operating margins (excluding stock-based compensation) were 11% This point about distillation is worth quoting in full (highlight mine): The start-up has also clamped down on “distillation” — a controversial practice whereby rival AI labs train their models on the outputs of more advanced ones. When rival companies “distil” their models from Anthropic’s models, that involves heavy usage and spending. Anthropic told investors on Wednesday distillation accounted for 5 per cent to 7 per cent of revenue and that they had cut it back “materially” in the third quarter of the year, said four people with direct knowledge of the matter. Napkin maths says that if distillation was 5% of their Q2 revenue (before they cut it back in Q3) then unnamed "other labs" spent over half a billion dollars distilling Anthropic's models in that quarter! Also notable: Anthropic appear to no longer be leaning on "annualized run-rate revenue" ( previously ) in these communications to their investors. Tags: ai , generative-ai , llms , anthropic

articles.title: AI is mass decompiling games. That's both awesome and scary.
articles.summary: AI is mass decompiling games. That's both awesome and scary. Indie game developer Popcar talks about the recent wave of AI-powered decompilation of existing games, enabling weird mashups between existing games, and producing a boom in game preservation projects to get old games working on new hardware (often in a browser using WebAssembly). I like how this piece captures both the positives and the negatives of this new development: Most people already realized the scary part by now. If AI can decompile games and software, then the entire tech industry is about to explode. Anybody can decompile other software and use it any way they'd like, and nobody can stop them. Companies can steal from competitors. Your paid game or app can be open-sourced against your will. This isn't exclusive to old video games, we can apply this to any software. [...] This is also a big win for preservation. Old games can be ported, modified, enhanced, and made much more easily accessible than before. [...[ With console makers going all in on digital and games becoming entirely unplayable due to servers shutting down, this is fantastic news. We could own software we bought regardless of what the company thinks. Via Hacker News Tags: computer-history , game-design , ai , webassembly , generative-ai , llms , ai-ethics , coding-agents

articles.title: Redesigning source control at Anthropic
articles.summary: Redesigning source control at Anthropic Interesting piece from Anthropic describing why and how they built their own custom alternative to Git, based on the dramatic increase in rate of changes to their code after the past six months. In May 2026, Anthropic averaged around 2,500 code changes merged per day; as of September, we merged over 30,000 per day. They included a chart showing those changes. I had Claude modify their chart ( code here ) to add markers for the public releases of each of their models in 2026: This shows public release dates, not the date when models became available for Anthropic's internal use. My guess is that the introduction of Fable/Mythos class models is a key factor in the increased coding velocity. "Antique" is their new code review system. The source control system is called Scion, and sounds to me like a reinvention of centralized source control along the lines of Subversion. ( Update : Anthropic credit Google's Piper and Meta's Sapling as "prior art" - it looks like the core concept of "derived data" was heavily inspired by Mononoke , the server component of Sapling.) They had some pretty extreme requirements: The history of our main branch alone is almost 100 GB, and a compressed working copy is over 25 GB. We perform on the order of 25 million code checkouts per day for CI, before counting developer environments, agent sandboxes, and research jobs. Fetched naively, that would be over 600 PB of git traffic per day. The new system was built by a team of seven people, and the migration from Git was completed in five months. When asked on Hacker News about the lack of offline support, Scion engineer Nick G replied : Since Claude is by far the heaviest user of Scion and is necessarily online, this just wasn't important to do. As an aside, I've been trying adversarial review in my own projects recently, where you have a model try and find flaws (I often play Claude and GPT off against each other). This note from the article reflected my own experience with that: Anthropic also makes extensive use of adversarial review, and, while this is incredibly effective in many ways, it can also be myopic, so skilled engineers needed to steer Claude away from over-engineering parts of the system in response to hypothetical concerns. Via Hacker News Tags: git , migrations , version-control , ai , generative-ai , llms , anthropic , agentic-engineering

articles.title: Hello Python 3.15, goodbye 3.10, and now I can use 3.11
articles.summary: Python 3.15 is here ! Here's the essential What's new in Python 3.15 guide, this year curated by 3.14 and 3.15 release manager Hugo van Kemenade. As someone who builds open source software that works in every supported Python version, I get to say goodbye to Python 3.10 and start embracing features from Python 3.11. First, some highlights from Python 3.15. Explicit lazy imports I'm most excited about Explicit lazy imports from PEP 810 . These let you import modules like so: lazy import json lazy from pathlib import Path The module will then be imported the first time those symbols are used in the code that follows. My LLM CLI tool implements plugins. I had to recommend manual lazy imports in the plugin author documentation, because simply installing plugins that used heavy dependencies such as sentence_transformers could add multiple seconds to every invocation of the llm command. Lazy imports directly address this startup cost. Unpacking in comprehensions The new [*sublist for sublist in lists] unpacking syntax is neat. Here's an illustration lifted from the documentation : lists = [[ 1 , 2 ], [ 3 , 4 ], [ 5 ]] [ * L for L in lists ] # [1, 2, 3, 4, 5] # equivalent to [x for L in lists for x in L] sets = [{ 1 , 2 }, { 2 , 3 }, { 3 , 4 }] { * s for s in sets } # {1, 2, 3, 4} # equivalent to {x for s in sets for x in s} dicts = [{ 'a' : 1 }, { 'b' : 2 }, { 'a' : 3 }] { ** d for d in dicts } # {'a': 3, 'b': 2} # equivalent to {k: v for d in dicts for k,v in d.items()} PEP 798: Unpacking in Comprehensions by Adam Hartz and Erik Demaine proposed this as an extension of the unpacking syntax from PEP 448 , which landed in Python 3.5 back in 2015. A sampling profiler Python's existing tracing profiler has been renamed from cProfile to profiling.tracing , and has been joined by an exciting new sampling profiler called Tachyon, aka profiling.sampling . Sampling profilers work by periodically capturing stack traces from running processes, then using those to calculate which functions have the most time spent inside of them. They're very low overhead and can provide a deep insight into running systems, without needing to instrument those systems first. I've previously used tools like py-spy for this. Now this capability is baked into the standard library. If you have the PID of an existing Python 3.15 process you can start gathering samples by running this (I had to use sudo on macOS): sudo uv run --python 3.15 python -m profiling.sampling attach 1234 Interact with the main program a bit, then hit Ctrl+C to stop gathering and see a report, which looks something like this: It can also produce flame graphs like this and heat maps like this , and can even output a format that can be viewed in the Firefox profiler UI. 3.15 isn't much faster than 3.14 Miguel Grinberg investigated How fast is Python 3.15? the other day against the 3.15.0rc3 release and found performance to be mostly the same as 3.14, with the exception of the experimental JIT. The JIT gave a 1.2x boost over the standard 3.15 interpreter (on a Fibonacci test), the first time Miguel observed a meaningful JIT performance increase. Miguel's explorations of 3.14 last year found significant boosts against Python 3.13 across many more categories. Upgrading to Python 3.15 with uv I used the following sequence of commands to get uv to use Python 3.15 on my Mac. First I had to upgrade uv itself to ensure it knew about the new release: uv self update Then I installed the stable 3.15 release: uv python install 3.15 And told uv that I wanted that to be the default for every uv run command, unless the project itself pinned a different version: uv python pin --global 3.15 Now the following reports 3.15 as the version: uv run python --version I already have a bunch of tools installed using uv tool install . I reinstalled them to use Python 3.15 like this: uv tool upgrade datasette --python 3.15 Then I can confirm the version like this: datasette --get /-/versions.json | jq Highlights from Python 3.11 The release of 3.15 means that Python 3.10 (released in 2021) is officially no longer supported . My policy for my main open source projects is to keep them working in every supported Python version. I can now drop 3.10 and start using features that were introduced in 3.11. Here's the What's new in Python 3.11 document. I finally get to rely on tomllib being available! Datasette makes extensive use of asyncio . 3.11 adds TaskGroup and timeout() , and several more new features. datetime.UTC is a new in 3.11 alias for datetime.timezone.utc . Python's SQLite support got some significant upgrades in 3.11, including: setlimit() and getlimit() expose a mechanism for setting SQLite runtime limits from Python. create_window_function() lets us create custom window functions in Python, as a class with step() , value() , inverse() , and finalize() methods. blobopen() provides an efficient mechanism for partial reads and writes of large BLOB binary values stored in a SQLite row. You can now call set_authorizer(None) to remove a SQLite authorizer. Datasette had a workaround for this! Plus a whole bunch of improvements to Python's typing system . I plan to land Python 3.11 improvements to a bunch of my projects over the next few weeks. Here's my first Datasette PR removing that set_authorizer(None) workaround. I've also updated my click-app , datasette-plugin , python-lib , and llm-plugin cookiecutter templates to test against Python 3.11 through Python 3.15. articles.title: Vercel Ship 2026 recap
articles.summary: For a decade, Vercel has shaped how the web is built. Now, we’re doing the same for agents. The companies that win the next decade will build on infrastructure designed for agents from the start, and thousands of people gathered across London, Berlin, New York, Sydney, and San Francisco to do just that at Vercel Ship 2026.Agentic infrastructureGuillermo Rauch (CEO, Vercel) opened Ship SF with a vision for the next era of software and agentic infrastructure: interfaces generated for any task in front of you, agents that reproduce and fix bugs autonomously, and software that takes production context and continuously improves itself.Agentic infrastructure has three parts:Vercel is where coding agents deploy software. When you ask your harness where to deploy, you get Vercel, because Vercel is built for the way agents work. We have over 200 CLI commands that your agent can use to operate our entire platform.Vercel is where you build and deploy your own agents. We give you every tool you need to build and run apps and agents in production, securely, at scale.Vercel itself is automated by agents. Vercel runs your apps in production, handling traffic, traces, observability, and anomalies. That data gives our agents the context they need to investigate autonomously, and then surface pull requests, not just alerts.Vercel exists to put the full force of agentic infrastructure behind you, so that you, your agents, and your software can deploy and run faster than ever. Vercel is for shipping full-stack apps and agentsIn the next keynote, Malte Ubl (CTO, Vercel) showed how frontends, APIs, backend services, containers, MCP servers, and background workers can all run on Vercel, with support for custom runtimes and system dependencies.He then announced that Python is now generally available on Vercel. Run FastAPI, Flask, or Django with standard CPython, PyPI dependencies, uv, and pyproject.toml. With Vercel Services, your frontend and backend deploy together, with previews of the full app.Malte also introduced Vercel Daemons, now in public beta, for continuously running background workers. Deploy your code or container image, set the number of instances, and Vercel keeps them running and replaces them if they fail. Bring Celery, Dramatiq, Temporal workers, or your existing worker processes.Vercel is for shipping agentsTomo Occhino (CPO, Vercel) walked through the Agent Stack and its latest updates. The Agent Stack gives you everything you need to build, run, and scale agents in production. eve, our open-source framework for building agents, now has persistent memory across sessions, extensions for installing tools and skills, and agent creation and deployment from the Vercel dashboard. Vercel Connect is generally available, with more than 1,000 connectors. And MCP Events, now in public beta, lets agents respond to events from MCP servers. Connect handles subscriptions, renewals, and secure delivery.AI Gateway now lets you set budgets for API keys, projects, individuals, and teams. You can also choose US-only inference to keep model processing in the United States, or enable Zero Data Retention so providers don’t retain your prompts or responses. He also introduced Vercel Token Pass, now in early access for Pro teams. Get $80 in GLM 5.3 and Kimi K3 token credit for $30/month, with more models coming soon.Vercel Drives, now generally available for Sandbox, gives agents persistent workspaces. Code, data, and saved memory survive across runs, so you can change runtimes or compute without rebuilding the workspace.Vercel is for shipping in the enterpriseJeanne Grosser (COO, Vercel) focused on what happens when everyone in a company can build. Engineers, marketers, analysts, and sellers need a common place to deploy, with controls over who can ship, who can access an app, which systems agents can use, and how much they can spend. Company building is now agent building.Vercel for Enterprise brings those controls together, with two additions announced:Bring Your Own Cloud on AWS is now generally available. Your application functions run in your own AWS account, within your security and network boundaries.Enterprise-Managed Authorization for Vercel Connect launched in public beta. With supported services and your identity provider configured, agents can act on employees’ behalf without asking each person to authorize every connection separately.Ship 2026 in San FranciscoThe rest of Ship SF brought more than 2,700 developers, founders, and technical leaders to the Palace of Fine Arts for talks, workshops, startup studio sessions, and agent labs.Ship day sessionsAssaf Elovic from Ora showed how his team tests whether websites work for agents by sending real agents to sign up, integrate, and pay, then tracing every step. Ora built that fleet on eve and used Is-Agentic to score a live site.Katelyn Lesse from Anthropic covered the work that starts after an agent is running: keeping it fast and improving its performance across thousands of production sessions with Claude Managed Agents on Vercel.Prashant Ratanchandani from Meta Superintelligence Labs joined Tomo to discuss building products including Muse on Vercel.Matt Lewis from Vercel and Mala Neti from Slack explained how we built v, our internal agent, around Vercel’s own data and working practices. Connect and Passport secure its access, and Slack gives employees a place to use it where their work already happens.Max Peters from Adapta broke down the router behind Brazil’s largest generative AI platform. Built on AI Gateway, it serves 168 models through one integration, selects a model in under 200 milliseconds, and handles more than three million requests a day with automatic failover and per-user budgets.Sarah Sachs from Notion and Malte Ubl discussed how AI is changing the software teams build and the context agents need to do useful work.Olawale Oladehin from AWS walked through production patterns for agents on AWS and Vercel, from self-correcting agents to multi-agent orchestration, and how BYOC lets teams run application functions within their own AWS environment.Philip Miseldine and Sophia Levens from SAP showed how SAP is using v0, eve, and json-render to build generative interfaces, with a focus on consistent design and government requirements.Aaron Brown and Arty Vohmincevs from Mercor explained how hundreds of employees build internal tools without losing control of access or spending. Apps inherit a managed identity layer, while AI Gateway gives the team visibility into model usage and budgets.Yury Izrailevsky from ClickHouse traced the company’s path from an open-source analytics database to a platform spanning observability, AI engineering, and managed Postgres. His focus was how open source earns developer trust and helps infrastructure expand into new workloads.Panel: Fast AIDiogo Almeida, co-founder and CEO of TypeSafe AI, the company behind Jev, and Andrew Feldman, founder and CEO of Cerebras, joined Vercel for a discussion on model reliability, latency, and cost. The panel brought together the model and hardware sides of fast inference, from specialized models to wafer-scale chips.Closing fireside with Tobi LütkeGuillermo sat down with Tobi Lütke, CEO of Shopify, for "The Third Customer," a conversation about building for a world where agents research, compare, and buy products on people’s behalf.Guillermo Rauch: What excites you about agentic commerce?Tobi Lütke: It’s early, but the opportunity goes beyond handling purchases people already make. Think about project-based commerce: planning Halloween decorations for your house, or a 3D-printing project with your kids, then ordering everything to arrive before the weekend. Agents can help people follow through on things they otherwise wouldn’t have had time to do.Guillermo Rauch: Where does that leave traditional storefronts?Tobi Lütke: There’s still room for exceptional shopping experiences. A distinctive, thoughtful storefront can grow, just as a well-executed boutique can. The businesses that will struggle are the ones offering an undifferentiated experience. Quality and originality still matter.Guillermo Rauch: How is AI changing engineering at Shopify?Tobi Lütke: We now think of ourselves as verification engineers, building harnesses and acceptance tests that make changes verifiable. We’re rewriting our storefront renderer from Ruby to Rust, where we can compare the output byte for byte before switching over. We also celebrate simplification and code deletion. At a company hackathon, our internal Slack agent, River, topped the code-deletion leaderboard by a wide margin.Guillermo Rauch: What should developers in this room go build?Tobi Lütke: Explore the catalog APIs. They give you access to products from Shopify merchants, so you can build new commerce experiences without first recruiting both sides of a marketplace. Product discovery, recommendations, and curation are real business opportunities. People will pay for tools that help them find what they need.Ship week San FranciscoFast Forward hackathonThe day before Ship, Vercel and Meta hosted Fast Forward, with support from Shopify and Neon Postgres. Builders worked across three tracks: agents that keep working after you step away, multimodal apps, and immersive VR experiences.Founder dinners, executive conversations, and Partner DayFounders, partners, and enterprise leaders gathered throughout the week for dinners, Partner Day, and conversations on building with AI. The executive program focused on what happens when anyone with an idea can build, and how do you govern what ships.Ship 2026 in London Ship day keynotesTomo introduced the Agent Stack, bringing model access, durable execution, sandboxed compute, and messaging together for production agents.Hedi launched Vercel Connect in public preview, giving agents scoped access to external tools and data without storing long-lived provider credentials in environment variables.Shar demoed eve, our open-source agent framework. Each agent lives in a directory, with instructions in Markdown and tools in TypeScript. Durable execution, approvals, subagents, and evals are already wired in.Jeanne introduced Vercel for Enterprise Apps and Agents, including Vercel Passport in public beta for protecting internal apps with your identity provider, and Bring Your Own Cloud on AWS in private beta.Ship week LondonOur first Ship outside the U.S. ran five days of events leading into the keynote, and an ice cream truck spent the week working its way across the city.Built in London hackathonTwo hundred builders shipped agents on Codex and Vercel in a hackathon with OpenAI. Three projects stood out. Stella hunts down unclaimed grants for London SMBs, Oscar is a co-pilot that sharpens your prompts before you send them to a model, and Phone Jail blocks distractions and roasts you when you reach for your phone anyway.Media, Founder, VC, and CTO dinnersReporters traded story ideas over a media dinner. Twelve founders talked through the future of AI in EMEA at a VC dinner. And a dozen CTOs from teams including Marks & Spencer and Currys went off the record on what it takes to build and scale agents in the enterprise. Day Zero builder nightDay Zero, the day before the keynote, turned into a 400-person builder night. Enterprise teams Mentimeter, Okta, and MongoDB joined Vercel in a packed room alongside partners DeepMind, ElevenLabs, and Cursor.AI Social ClubA 160-deep waitlist formed for Malte's talk A New Stack for a New Era of Software, followed by Guillermo and Deliveroo's Will Shu's chat on building the agentic enterprise.Ship day sessionsAndré Balleyguier from Anthropic showed Claude Managed Agents on Vercel, where Anthropic hosts the agent loop while every command the agent runs executes inside a Vercel Sandbox you own, keeping its filesystem, processes, and network egress in your environment.Tomas Jansson from Currys/Elkjøp showed how his team evolved a Nordic retailer's ecommerce stack from storefronts toward shopping agents in three phases, anchored by a Next.js migration that cut time to first byte by 40%. The end state is one where customer intent replaces navigation.Matan Kushner from Vercel broke down how Vertex, Vercel's support agent, now automates 91% of support tickets and saves 5,000 engineer-hours a month without degrading as its context grows. Jas Sagoo and Sam Bellen from Auth0 made the case that getting an agent into production depends more on identity than on model quality. They demoed four standards-based identity patterns on the Vercel AI SDK, Token Vault, CIBA approvals, agents as first-class principals, and on-behalf-of delegation, so every action is scoped and traces back to a human decision instead of a shared API key.Abhi Sivasailam from Vercel went deep into d0, Vercel's internal data agent built on eve, which runs analyses in a sandbox and now gets 45% of its questions from other agents, rather than people.Romain Huet from OpenAI showed developers how to ship faster by delegating whole tasks to Codex Cloud Agents on Vercel, and made the case that as agents become users of your product, you design for agent experience with scoped API keys, markdown docs, and plugins.Michał Pierzchała from Callstack demoed a QA agent that runs mobile apps on real devices, explores user flows on its own, and posts screenshots, recordings, and logs to pull requests on every PR.Alex Holt from ElevenLabs paired the ElevenLabs Speech Engine with the AI SDK to build a voice agent that can reply in under a second, take interruptions mid-sentence, and switch language mid-conversation.Malavika Balachandran Tadeusz from Vercel showed the mechanics of how software can ship itself, extending the agent loop past development into testing, observability, and experimentation with primitives like Vercel Flags and Skills.Panel: Agents in productionJeanne Grosser, COO of Vercel, moderated a panel on taking agentic workloads from prototype to production with some of the EU's top CTOs and AI leaders from frontier labs. A few highlights: Arthur Viegers (Cursor): Autonomy should track risk, and the better an agent can assess the risk of a change, the more you can let it run on its own. Shopify and Amplitude already auto-review and merge 60-70% of low-risk PRs with no developer time, while a two-line change to authentication still goes to a human.André Balleyguier (Anthropic): To decide what an agent can do on its own, judge each action by how reversible it is and how large its blast radius is, then contain it accordingly, for example inside a self-hosted sandbox. As you grant more autonomy, observability and evals become the things that keep it safe.Ryan den Rooijen (Currys): The predicted death of stores never arrived, and Currys leads its markets by betting on humans. The open question for agentic commerce is which shopping journeys customers want an agent to handle and which they still want a person for.Nicolas Le Pallec (AKQA): AI-native customer experience replaces navigation with intent. Reaching it takes three layers: a way to capture true customer intent, a brand brain that stores brand and product data for AI systems to retrieve, and generative UI that composes pages on the fly instead of serving static ones.Fireside chat with Harry StebbingsThe day ended with a fireside chat between Guillermo and Harry Stebbings from 20VC. Below are excerpts from the lightning round at the end of the discussion. Guillermo Rauch: What are the attributes of a founder you want to back?Harry Stebbings: The profile has changed completely. It used to be a sales-led CEO who could fundraise and grow customers, where personality and sales carried the company. Now I want an engineering- and product-led founder.Guillermo Rauch: Can you teach someone to become a voice for their industry?Harry Stebbings: You can, but it's hard. You have to do it for six months straight. It's a muscle you build, and you have to commit to it every day and every hour.Guillermo Rauch: When anyone can produce content and software, how do you stand out?Harry Stebbings: You come up with a new format, a new intro, a new way to tell the story and shape the work. The content itself has shifted too. We used to do shows about leadership and hiring, and nobody cares about that anymore. What lands now is a founder and AI. Those are the two things.Ship 2026 in Berlin The Berlin event opened at the Old Mint, “Alte Münze”, where coins were once hammered by hand, before machine automation took over. It is also where the JavaScript logo was born, and where Guillermo Rauch (CEO) met Malte Ubl (CTO) for the first time at JSConf EU.Software is moving the same way, from hand to machine, and Vercel is paving the way for building in the agentic era. Over 500 people gathered from across Germany to do just that at Ship 2026 in Berlin.Ship day sessionsSuyog Rao from Vercel announced AI SDK 7. The AI SDK is now downloaded over 16 million times a week. Version 7 turns it into a toolkit for building and running agents that reason, call tools, run across many turns, and work across files and sandboxes, all behind one provider-agnostic interface with no lock-in.Philip Miseldine from SAP showed how the company rebuilt its design system to be composable, so people and agents assemble interfaces from the same parts, with v0 running across its build, deliver, and decide stages.Building with AI SDK 7 brought three speakers on stage. Lars Grammel, the primary engineer behind the update, went deep on the release, with the new harness layer and generation beyond text as the headline additions. Carsten Høyer from AKQA demoed the Starbucks ChatGPT app as a "generative store" that composes branded results from Starbucks' own products and visual identity, flipping the funnel so customers pull the brand into their conversation instead of visiting its site. Stephen Batifol from Black Forest Labs showed where the Flux image models fit in an agentic stack: sub-second generation and editing today, heading toward real-time generation and world models.Arthur Viegers from Cursor showed how coding agents move from autocomplete to working across an entire codebase on their own.Panel: CTOs on AI and growthChris Williams (Head of Forward Deployed Engineering, Vercel) moderated a CTO panel on building and scaling as the cost of creation trends toward zero. A few highlights:Sven Rosemann (Flaconi): AI won't fix a broken business model, so the work is still operational excellence. He compares ecommerce to a decathlon, you win by being top-tier across every discipline at once. What's changing is discovery, which is moving into chat, so Flaconi is investing in the data foundation that makes its catalog retrievable by agents, betting that buying and checkout eventually happen there too.Tjaž Silovsek (Astra AI): venture funding is no longer a prerequisite. For many ideas, you ship, find distribution, and iterate instead. Astra reached 10 million users and $25M ARR fully bootstrapped, with a small team kept fast by a stable foundation and agents given a lot of autonomy while kept as safe as possible.DACH Partner AwardVercel presented its first-ever DACH Partner Award to Valtech, for the exceptional impact and delivery, strategic thinking and team enablement it brought to clients. The presentation also thanked the event's sponsors: Auth0, Storyblok, Cursor, SAP, Accenture Song, Blazity, and JVM.Ship 2026 in New YorkShip week New YorkShip NYC was the most in-demand of any stop yet with over 3,000 people registered. Founders, partners, leaders, and builders gathered for five days of hackathons, executive receptions, workshops, and more, with Ship day at the center.Built in NYCThe week opened with Built in NYC, a hackathon co-hosted by Vercel and Anthropic alongside Sentry, Auth0, Resend, and Supabase. More than one hundred people joined us for an afternoon of building and demoing agents on Vercel. VC, CTO, and VIP dinnersJeanne DeWitt Grosser and Nick Bogaty gathered the leaders shaping AI-native development at a VIP reception. Founders traded notes on the future of agents over a VC dinner. At Per Se, Guillermo, Jeanne, Tom, and Malte took CTOs and CIOs for a closed-door conversation on where traditional architectures start to break in the agent era.AI Social ClubAI executives and senior leaders assembled at Moss for a fireside chat led by Tom Occhino with William Anderson (CTO, Bloomberg Media), Jeremy Bunting (VP Engineering, Serhant), and Ali Patterson (Staff Design Program Manager, DoorDash). They discussed what's working, what's not, and where agentic infrastructure is driving meaningful outcomes for enterprises. Ship day sessionsRyan Coyne from SERHANT. walked through S.MPLE, a real estate agent built on Vercel that drove a 144% increase in commission income in its first full year.Brandon Bloom from Brex gave its expense-audit agent a bash-only shell so it manages its own context instead of drowning in tool responses, cutting tool calls and token usage by 75%.Ari Schapiro and Chris Sev from Auth0 demoed how to give an agent scoped, revocable power instead of a master key, with standards-based identity patterns like Token Vault and out-of-band human approval, live on the Vercel AI SDK.Jenny Wang from Alta and Maxwell Osborne from PUBLIC SCHOOL NYC showed how Alta's AI styling app runs on Vercel, generating an avatar a second and 250M+ outfits so far. Together they built a custom version for PUBLIC SCHOOL's New York Fashion Week relaunch.Charlton Roberts from FLORA showed three creative-production workflows running on Vercel Sandboxes. They collapsed 18 bespoke tools into two by letting the agent run and write its own code against the AI SDK.Prasad Wangikar from Stripe broke down how to give agents spending power and capture agent-driven revenue using emerging protocols like MCP, UCP, and x402 for the machine-to-machine economy.Shaown Nandi from AWS discussed how Vercel and AWS work together, with native AWS databases and OpenSearch available in the Marketplace and models through the AI Gateway, proven out by The Weather Company's 350M+ users.Panel: Internal apps and agents in productionJeanne moderated a panel on building and deploying internal agents with technical leaders on who should build, what governance looks like, and how teams can move from experiment to production. A few highlights:Andy Martin (MJH Life Sciences): The way to win the shadow-IT battle is to constrain the stack and stay permissive inside it. His AI Accelerator trains non-engineers, marketers, and early-career staff to build internal apps on a deliberately tight stack of Claude Code, Vercel, and GitHub, with ephemeral preview deployments as the guardrail. As he put it, "If it becomes the Department of No, you will have people working around you."Greg Chan (SERHANT): The cleanest way to structure agents is to mirror a human software team. Product-manager agents write requirements in Linear, engineering agents generate specs, and build-and-QA agents take it from there, so engineers become leads running multiple streams. To keep output safe, SERHANT runs evals for hallucination and compliance, including a custom model for Fair Housing Act rules.Victor Oliveros (ZoomInfo): Embedding v0 inside your own product lets your customers build their own workflows. At ZoomInfo, 40,000+ of them do, turning the voice of the customer into a pull request. Agents analyze recorded calls and open PRs, so the product team decides what ships instead of synthesizing feedback. They pair Vercel's deployment guardrails with ZoomInfo's context-graph permissions, so each agent only touches data its user can see.Fireside chat: Building agentic storefrontsTom sat down with Vanessa Lee (VP of Product, Shopify) to discuss where commerce and software go next. Below are highlights: Tom Occhino: Vercel and Shopify have shipped something new together. What is it?Vanessa Lee: We boiled Hydrogen down to the parts of commerce that are genuinely hard (analytics, optimistic cart UI, variants) and made them work with any framework. So if you're on Next.js on Vercel, Shopify's commerce primitives now drop in, with an integration in the Vercel Marketplace. Read more here.Tom Occhino: You also opened the Catalog API. What does it unlock?Vanessa Lee: There's never been a good open product-search API. We have billions of products and millions of merchants, so we built one, the only widespread shopping API, made for commerce. It lets anyone embed shopping anywhere. Someone in my Toronto running group used v0 to build a site with a leaderboard and the weather, and the Catalog API surfaced products from nearby stores. Commerce stops being a destination and becomes part of what you build.Tom Occhino: Shopify and Vercel both obsess over reducing friction. Why does that matter so much?Vanessa Lee: Early on, Tobi's insight was that tools shape the market. The TAM was never limited by demand, it was limited by how hard the tools were to use. Make building easier and more people build. There's resourcefulness in the general population that's just untapped, and lowering the friction is what releases it.Closing keynote with Ivan ZhaoWe closed out Ship in New York with a conversation between Guillermo Rauch and Ivan Zhao (CEO, Notion). A few highlights:Guillermo Rauch: You've started telling designers to design for the API first and the UI last. Why?Ivan Zhao: Because your next customer isn't only a human, it's a human and an agent, and agents are blind. They don't see your interface, they read your semantics and your API. The most enduring software has always been a data structure anyway, the spreadsheet, or our block, a data structure that happens to have a UI. So design the structure and the meaning first, the interface last. A great tool for developers turns out to be a great tool for agents.Guillermo Rauch: Vercel and Notion are both aggressively model-agnostic, Switzerland in the model wars. Why?Ivan Zhao: The models leapfrog each other every few weeks, so picking a side is a losing game. We route automatically by the intelligence a task needs, frontier models for coding, smaller and faster ones for support and summarization. What excites me most is that as more use cases stop needing frontier intelligence, you can shape smaller models to your product and win back speed and cost. And speed creates discontinuities, a model five times faster can change the kind of interface you'd even design.Guillermo Rauch: When a billion knowledge workers are agents, how does that reshape us?Ivan Zhao: We can't fully see it, and that's the point. First-order effects are easy, the iPhone was an iPod plus a phone plus a browser. The second-order effects are the ones that surprise you, like what social media did to teenagers. We shape our tools, and then our tools shape us. With software that can think, the second-order effects are the ones we won't predict.Guillermo Rauch: Taste or velocity, keep one.Ivan Zhao: Taste. It's the distillation of wisdom from a lot of shots on goal.Ship 2026 in Sydney The Sydney event opened at Machine Hall, a 1930s electrical substation that ran the city's trams and wharves for half a century. Over 200 people gathered there to build for the agentic era at Ship Sydney. Ship week SydneyThe week kicked off with the AI SYD meetup, where developers, AI engineers, and the Sydney technical community joined for an evening of lightning talks and networking. At the AI Social Club, senior leaders gathered at Shell House for a talk from Malte Ubl and a fireside with Suyog Rao and David Hyman (Founder, monō ai) on how agentic infrastructure is driving meaningful outcomes for enterprises.Ship day sessionsBelen Garcia Fava and Vivek Katial from Heidi Health showed how their team ships fast in a regulated space with agents and Vercel, and made the case that trust is engineered, not granted. Robin Yoong from Cursor created an eve agent by voice alone. Three models coded in parallel, and a spoken approval shipped it to Vercel.Nonny Bell (Startup Manager APAC, Vercel) moderated a panel with Matthew Blode (AI Engineer, Linktree), Aarush Issar (GM AI Engineering, Auto & General Australia), and Leonardo Borges (Chief Engineer Gen AI, CommBank) on how their teams are adopting AI agents in production.JJ Lecocq (Sales Director AUNZ, Vercel) led a discussion on how organizations are reshaping people, culture, and structure for AI.Ship what's nextThanks for joining us for Ship 2026 in London, Berlin, New York, Sydney, and San Francisco. We'll see you in May for Ship 2027. Read more

articles.title: Open weight takes 71.5% of tokens and 23% of spend
articles.summary: AI Gateway Production Index — October 2026Every month, AI Gateway routes tens of trillions of tokens between production applications and AI labs. That traffic gives us a view of what AI usage actually looks like in today's enterprise, and we publish it here monthly. See the Production Index reports from July, August, and September.October 2026 summary Open-weight models now process more than seven in ten gateway tokens and account for nearly one in four dollars. Their share of spend has more than quadrupled since June.September’s gateway spend was about 13 times December’s, while the average price per token was 47% lower. Almost one in three teams changed their most-used lab in September, an index record.Nearly 70% of September’s gateway spend on Chinese models went through US-based providers, up from less than 10% in December.Jev was the fastest-adopted model in AI Gateway history, reaching 35% of paid teams in its first two weeks, but it accounted for just 0.27% of gateway spend over that same period. Opus 5.5 took more than one in ten gateway dollars in its own first two weeks, the largest spend share of any September model launch.Frontier spend up 900%, spend share down 22%In August, open-weight models processed the majority of AI Gateway token volume for the first time. The money is now following. Open weight’s share of spend has more than quadrupled over the last three months, from one in twenty gateway dollars in June to nearly one in four in September.Open weight's growth is coming from both ends of its price range, and it mirrors the wider gateway. The cheapest models drive token growth, while the expensive models drive spend.Led by Kimi K3, models priced at least four times the open-weight average cost per token accounted for about two-thirds of the increase in open-weight spend.In contrast, DeepSeek-v4.1-Flash alone processed nearly half of all September tokens but took just 2.6% of spend. Its price per token was about a fifth of the open-weight average.Customers are increasing budgets on both sides of the market. Since December, spend on frontier models has grown tenfold; spend on open-weight models has grown more than seventyfold.In September, 68% of teams that put more money into open-weight models did the same for closed-weight models. And more than two in five teams already paying for frontier models spent more on them than in August, the highest share this year.Spending on the frontier is still growing, but spending on alternatives is growing faster. A company can spend more with a frontier lab while relying on it for fewer workloads, so the lab gets more money, but a smaller part of the customer’s business. AI spend increases 13x while the cost per token halvesMarket share is changing hands inside a market that is getting much bigger and cheaper.September's gateway spend was about 13 times December's, an increase of 1,180%, while the average price per token fell 47%. The median paid customer active in both December and September more than doubled its spend.Teams are spending more, but labs have to keep winning their business. In September, nearly one in two teams changed their most-used model. And almost one in three changed their most-used lab, an index record.Even teams with lower token volumes use a wide mix of models. Since December, teams that processed at least 10 million tokens over that period used an average of 15 different models. The average rose to 26 for teams processing at least 100 million tokens, and 42 for those processing at least a billion.The model is becoming a replaceable part of a much larger investment. Companies can continuously improve their AI products and workflows while changing which models power them. They can spend more on AI without becoming more dependent on any one lab.Chinese models are big business for American providersMore than two-thirds of September’s gateway spend on Chinese-origin models went to US-based providers, up from less than a tenth in December. The Chinese lab builds the model; the American provider runs it and sells access.DeepSeek’s models processed 58% of all gateway tokens for 6.6% of spend. More than four in five of those tokens were served by DeepSeek itself, yet two in five dollars spent on its models went through US-based providers.Moonshot AI, the Beijing-based lab behind Kimi, accounted for 3.6% of gateway tokens and 13.2% of spend in September. US-based providers served nine in ten of those tokens.Z.ai, also based in Beijing and the creator of GLM, accounted for 7.2% of all tokens and 4.5% of spend. US-based providers served seven in ten.Customers can use Chinese models through access sold by American providers. For teams that put more money into Chinese models in September, an average of 53% of their spending on those models went through US-based providers and 41% through China-based ones.The same Chinese model can compete with US-based models while generating revenue for US-based providers. September model launch scorecard: Jev, Opus 5.5, and GPT-6Whether a model launch is successful depends on what you measure: how broadly it’s tried, how much usage and spend it receives, or what share of its initial users return. We ranked every model launch in September with at least two weeks of data by these metrics; the tables show the top ten for each. The full scorecard is at the end of the report.Jev is the most-adopted and most-called modelIn its first two weeks, Jev reached more than a third of paid teams, nearly double the reach of Sonnet 5.5 in second place. This is the fastest adoption of any model in AI Gateway history. Jev also received the most requests of any model in September, even though it launched halfway through the month. Of the teams that tried Jev in week one, 55.6% returned in week two, the fifth-highest retention rate.Jev is a decision model. If someone can't see data in a source system, they can't access it through an app or agent either. Without a model router, that would require integrating with multiple separate providers, spreading API keys and budget management across platforms.AI Gateway gives you access to hundreds of models through a single API, with no markup on cost, and Zero Data Retention keeps your data from being stored or trained on. You can also elect to route through US-only providers to maintain compliance.How Mercor manages model governance at scaleMercor connects AI labs with subject-matter experts who help train and evaluate models. Their engineers need access to hundreds of models to enable that work, but before migrating to Vercel, access was spread across direct integrations and third-party routers, making stolen credentials a huge risk, and token spend impossible to manage.They moved their model routing to AI Gateway, and now engineers can access hundreds of models with a single, expiring secret, and they can set budgets per person or project.In their first 10 days on AI Gateway, they processed 63 billion tokens without hitting any rate limits.Centralized visibility and securityVercel Observability gives you a single view for app and agent telemetry across every project, so you can easily manage performance and troubleshoot problems for both internal tools and customer-facing products.The Security Dashboard flags risks across your team and apps, including missing MFA, unprotected preview deployments, long-lived credentials, and framework vulnerabilities. With BYOC, application functions execute in your AWS account, within your security and network boundaries.Meta Superintelligence Labs runs on Vercel via BYOC, giving its AI teams the ability to test and deploy ideas quickly, inside their own AWS environment. Leaders at Meta said that in their first week on Vercel, they shipped a month worth of work.From idea to global scale on one platformVercel let's everyone in your company build safely, and makes it easy for engineers to ship the best ideas at global scale, all on a single platform.That is how we built Vertex, our customer support agent. articles.title: Introducing Vercel Drives: persistent storage for agents
articles.summary: Agents often handle complex work that continues across runs. As that work evolves, they may need a new environment with different tools, runtimes, or compute. They should be able to continue working with the same files when they change environments.We built Vercel Drives to keep an agent’s files independent of its execution environment. It is now generally available for Vercel Sandbox. Agents can mount the same drive in a new environment configured for the next task and continue where they left off.Persisting state with a driveCreate a drive once, then mount it when you create a sandbox. From the CLI:Or from the Sandbox SDK:In this example, everything under /workspace persists on the drive. Everything else belongs to the sandbox. The next sandbox that mounts the drive finds the repository, and anything else the agent wrote there, where the previous run left it.The drive keeps the agent’s files independent of the sandbox running it. An agent can resume work in a new sandbox or switch runtimes without transferring its workspace. Other sandboxes can mount the same drive.Sharing state across sandboxesAgents can prepare files on a drive once and reuse them across sandboxes. articles.title: Python on Vercel is now generally available
articles.summary: Python on Vercel is now generally available. Build and run Python applications with the frameworks, libraries, and tools you already use.Vercel automatically detects supported frameworks and configures the build and deployment. Your applications run on Fluid compute, which manages concurrent requests and scales with traffic. Idiomatic Python SDKs let you work with storage, queues, durable workflows, and AI models directly from Python. For full-stack projects, the Python backend and frontend share a workflow for local development, preview deployments, and production releases.Our goals for Python on VercelTen months ago, we set out to make Vercel the best place to build and run Python applications. We wanted the experience to fit how Python developers already work, with three goals guiding our decisions:Idiomatic Python SDKs. Working with Vercel infrastructure should feel familiar to Python developers, with APIs that use type annotations, async/await, and context managers.A shared workflow for both the frontend and backend. Python applications often include a JavaScript frontend, so developers should be able to run both locally, review them in the same preview deployment, and release or roll them back together.Compatibility with the Python ecosystem. The runtime should use CPython, the standard Python interpreter, on Linux to preserve compatibility with the packages and tools Python developers already rely on.The first test of those goals is what happens when you deploy a Python application on Vercel: its framework, dependencies, and project structure should guide how it’s built and run.Deploying Python applications on VercelWe’ve worked to make Python feel native on Vercel. Vercel reads your project’s dependency files, including those managed by uv, and automatically detects frameworks such as FastAPI, Flask, Django, and FastHTML. Framework defined infrastructure configures builds and request routing, with framework-specific support for serving static assets through the CDN.For applications with a frontend, Vercel Services brings both parts into one project. Running vercel dev starts them together, and shared previews let you test backend changes with the frontend that uses them.For long-running workers that pull jobs from queues or databases, Vercel Daemons keeps your containers running with your Python code along with any of its packages, and system dependencies.Python SDKs for Vercel infrastructureA Python backend might need to store files, send messages, run durable workflows, or call AI models. We’ve built Python SDKs for these tasks, with APIs that follow the conventions of the language:These SDKs work alongside your framework and libraries, and the example below shows how they connect within a full-stack application.Start building with Python on VercelWhether you’re starting a new project or deploying existing code, the framework guides cover setup and deployment on Vercel. For a guided full-stack project, the Python on Vercel course walks through building a FastAPI backend and Next.js frontend, then deploying them together with Services.To show how these pieces work together, I built a collaborative web application to create and browse Python notebooks. It lets people create their own notebooks, publish them for others to browse or fork, and work with an AI assistant to write and run Python code.The application pairs a Vite frontend with a FastAPI backend and uses PostgreSQL for notebook source and chat history. Services keeps the frontend and backend in one deployment, with the frontend served through the CDN.Here’s how the main parts connect:Editing and running code: When a signed-in user opens their notebook in the editor, FastAPI creates or reuses a Vercel Sandbox running Jupyter, keeping user code isolated from the application backend. The browser connects directly to Jupyter, while mounted Drives provide the Python dependencies and workspace files.Saving and publishing: The browser periodically sends the current notebook to FastAPI. FastAPI saves the source in PostgreSQL, renders changes as HTML, and uploads the result to Blob, so people can read published notebooks through the CDN without starting a Python kernel.Sharing updates: After publishing a change, FastAPI sends a message through Vercel Queues. Each backend instance with connected browsers receives the notification and sends updated notebook listings over WebSockets, so people see changes without reloading.Assisting with code: The agent uses AI SDK for Python and runs inside Vercel Workflows, which saves execution state and retries failed steps. Chat history stays in PostgreSQL, while notebook editing and execution tools work through the connected browser, which sends results back through FastAPI to resume the workflow.The source code on GitHub includes the complete application and its deployment configuration. You can use it to explore these integrations or as a starting point for your own Python application.Investing in the Python communityLast December, the Gel Data team, led by me and Elvis Pranskevichus, joined Vercel to build Python support and continue our open-source work.At the same time, we announced our sponsorship of the Python Software Foundation and committed to funding one year of Serhiy Storchaka’s CPython maintenance through the foundation. Serhiy has authored over 600 commits to CPython’s main branch so far in 2026.We also sponsored PyCon US and EuroPython this year, where the team and I met Python developers and heard where they were getting stuck. Those conversations help us figure out what to fix next.We also published PEP 827, which, if accepted, would add type manipulation features that could help frameworks such as FastAPI offer simpler APIs with less boilerplate and more precise type checking.What’s next for Python on VercelWe’re continuing to improve Python SDKs, runtime performance, and development workflows for both people and coding agents. If you run into a deployment issue or find something missing in the Python SDKs, share your feedback in Vercel Community so the team can use it to guide that work.ResourcesPoint your agent at our Python guides in the Knowledge BaseDeploy an eve agent in Python in one click Read more
